title: Experimental Ebola vaccine enters first human trial as Congo outbreak worsens
summary: Researchers in Oxford have begun the first human trial of an experimental vaccine targeting the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola as the Democratic Republic of Congo reports 3,200 confirmed cases and 1,405 deaths. The vaccine, built on the Oxford-AstraZeneca COVID platform, will enroll 50 volunteers in an initial safety and immunogenicity study. Further small trials are planned in Uganda, followed by a larger efficacy trial in the DRC if results are promising.
content:
The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has reported 3,200 confirmed Ebola cases and 1,405 deaths, according to government data, underscoring the severity of an outbreak that continues to challenge health services and aid agencies.

In response, researchers in the United Kingdom have launched the first human trial of an experimental vaccine designed to protect against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola linked to the current outbreak. The first volunteer, 37-year-old Ed Hunt from the UK, was inoculated in Oxford as part of an early-stage clinical study. Hunt said he volunteered after following reports from the DRC and wanting to "do my bit." He is the first of 50 healthy volunteers aged 18 to 55 who will take part in the initial trial.

The candidate vaccine was developed by the University of Oxford team using the same viral vector platform employed for the Oxford-AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. Scientists report they produced the vaccine candidate in about eight weeks, drawing on decades of prior infectious-disease and vaccine research. Professor Teresa Lambe, who leads the Oxford vaccine team, said the platform allowed a rapid response to the outbreak.

Researchers emphasize that the new vaccine targets the Bundibugyo strain and that the existing licensed vaccine covers the Zaire strain only, offering no protection against Bundibugyo. That gap has accelerated development of multiple Bundibugyo-targeted candidates; the Oxford vaccine is the first of four such candidates to enter human testing.

The phase one trial will focus on safety and whether the vaccine provokes a strong immune response that might be protective. "We will not be giving anybody Ebola in this trial or any trial," Lambe said, stressing that the vaccine cannot cause Ebola infection. The primary goals are to establish safety and measure immunogenicity.

Following the Oxford study, researchers plan a second small trial in Uganda before moving to a larger efficacy trial in the DRC if early results justify expansion. The Serum Institute of India has already manufactured 600,000 doses to allow rapid deployment should the vaccine prove effective. Funding from organizations including CEPI has helped speed development and testing.

For communities contending with a growing outbreak and a rising death toll, scientists and public health officials hope the vaccine, if safe and effective, will become an important tool to control transmission and prevent further loss of life.

content.author: Chigozie Ohaka

## Outbreak Overview

The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has reported 3,200 confirmed Ebola cases and 1,405 deaths, according to government data, underscoring the severity of an outbreak that continues to challenge health services and aid agencies.

## UK Human Trial Launch

In response, researchers in the United Kingdom have launched the first human trial of an experimental vaccine designed to protect against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola linked to the current outbreak. The first volunteer, 37-year-old Ed Hunt from the UK, was inoculated in Oxford as part of an early-stage clinical study. Hunt said he volunteered after following reports from the DRC and wanting to “do my bit.” He is the first of 50 healthy volunteers aged 18 to 55 who will take part in the initial trial.

## Vaccine Development

The candidate vaccine was developed by the University of Oxford team using the same viral vector platform employed for the Oxford-AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. Scientists report they produced the vaccine candidate in about eight weeks, drawing on decades of prior infectious-disease and vaccine research. Professor Teresa Lambe, who leads the Oxford vaccine team, said the platform allowed a rapid response to the outbreak.

## Target Strain and Multiple Candidates

Researchers emphasize that the new vaccine targets the Bundibugyo strain and that the existing licensed vaccine covers the Zaire strain only, offering no protection against Bundibugyo. That gap has accelerated development of multiple Bundibugyo-targeted candidates; the Oxford vaccine is the first of four such candidates to enter human testing.

## Trial Focus and Safety

The phase one trial will focus on safety and whether the vaccine provokes a strong immune response that might be protective.

> “We will not be giving anybody Ebola in this trial or any trial,” Lambe said, stressing that the vaccine cannot cause Ebola infection.

The primary goals are to establish safety and measure immunogenicity.

## Next Steps and Manufacturing

Following the Oxford study, researchers plan a second small trial in Uganda before moving to a larger efficacy trial in the DRC if early results justify expansion. The Serum Institute of India has already manufactured 600,000 doses to allow rapid deployment should the vaccine prove effective. Funding from organizations including CEPI has helped speed development and testing.

## Outlook

For communities contending with a growing outbreak and a rising death toll, scientists and public health officials hope the vaccine, if safe and effective, will become an important tool to control transmission and prevent further loss of life.
